report.summary: The demo-service DB connection pool saturated at its hard cap, requests began queueing for a connection, and the resulting acquire timeouts surfaced as a spike of 5xx responses and p95 HTTP latency, firing both the latency and error-ratio rules. Saturation and queueing preceded any HTTP error or latency degradation, and the only error log pattern is connection-acquire timeouts, so pool exhaustion is the most probable cause; the demand ramp that consumed the pool and DB-side operation latency remain unchecked.

timeline.event: Pool usage starts at {used_first} connections and begins climbing; p95 latency still at baseline {lat_base} s.
Pool usage reaches the ceiling of {used_max} connections; pending requests jump to {pending_max} and p95 connection wait rises to {wait_mid} s.
First sampled error log: 'request failed' / 'timeout exceeded when trying to connect' from version 1.0.1.
Connection-acquire timeouts appear at {to_first} timeouts/s; 5xx ratio reaches {err_at_0910} and p95 latency jumps to {lat_at_0910} s.
Peak degradation: p95 latency {lat_max} s, 5xx ratio {err_max}, pool wait p95 {wait_max} s, timeouts at {to_max} timeouts/s, pool used {used_max} against pool_max {pmax}.

hypotheses.statement: Exhaustion of the hard-capped DB connection pool (pool_max {pmax}) caused the incident: demand drove pool usage to {used_max} connections, up to {pending_max} requests queued for a connection with p95 wait of {wait_max} s, and connection-acquire timeouts at {to_max} timeouts/s produced the 5xx ratio of {err_max} and p95 latency of {lat_max} s.

Slowness of the database dependency elevated per-query time, so each connection was held longer and the connection pool was consumed, with client-visible p95 latency reaching {lat_max} s and 5xx ratio {err_max}.
A surge in incoming request demand (rather than per-query slowness) consumed the pool: pending requests reached {pending_max} while pool usage was pinned at {used_max} against a cap of {pmax}.

observations.statement: Pool usage climbed monotonically from {used_first} to {used_max} connections and hit the pool ceiling by the end of the window.
The pool ceiling pool_max was flat at {pmax} connections for every step of the incident window, so the pool was hard-capped, not resized.
In the baseline window before the incident, pool usage was at most {used_base_max} connections.
Requests waiting for a connection jumped from {pending_min} to {pending_max} requests at 18:08:55 and stayed there.
p95 connection wait climbed from a {wait_min} s baseline to {wait_mid} s at 18:08:55 and then {wait_max} s at 18:09:25.
Connection-acquire timeout rate went from {to_first} timeouts/s at 18:09:10 to {to_max} timeouts/s at 18:09:25.
The 5xx ratio was {err_early} at 18:07:10 and rose to {err_at_0910} at 18:09:10, then {err_max} at 18:09:25.
HTTP p95 latency held near {lat_base} s through 18:08:55 and then broke to {lat_at_0910} s at 18:09:10 and {lat_max} s at 18:09:25.

The only error log pattern in the window was 'request failed' with exception 'timeout exceeded when trying to connect', {p1_count} sampled lines between 18:09:08.821Z and 18:09:25.841Z, all from service version 1.0.1.
Error log volume only appears in the 18:09 minute bucket, starting at {err_vol_first} and rising to {err_vol_last} in the following bucket, while warn and info volumes stay low and flat.

recommendations.action: Raise pool_max above {pmax} connections (and verify the database can serve the higher concurrency) or add admission control/queueing in front of DB calls so acquire waits do not become HTTP errors.
recommendations.rationale: Pool usage was pinned at the hard cap of {pmax} with up to {pending_max} waiting requests and timeouts at {to_max} timeouts/s, so headroom or bounded queueing would prevent acquire timeouts from surfacing as 5xx.

recommendations.action: Investigate the demand ramp between 18:07:10 and 18:08:55 that consumed the pool, including retry storms or a traffic burst on the callers of demo-service.
recommendations.rationale: Pending requests reached {pending_max} while pool usage climbed to {used_max}, which points at a surge in concurrent work rather than an isolated slow query.

recommendations.action: Query db_operation_p95 and DB-side latency for the same window to rule out per-query slowness holding connections.
recommendations.rationale: The dependency-latency hypothesis (hyp_2) could not be tested because the metric query hit the budget limit (ev_10); per-query latency data would confirm or dismiss it.
